newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: POLICE CLOSING IN ON PERTH SERIAL KILLER
Police in Perth believe they're closing in on a serial killer believed to be responsible for the murders of at least two women.
They say they've gained vital clues from the scene where the body of Perth lawyer, Ciara Glennon, was found yesterday.
Her remains were found by a bushwalker at Eglinton, 40 kilometres north of the city, and not far south from the Yanchep National Park.
Three weeks ago, Ms Glennon became the third woman to vanish from the Claremont nightstrip in the past 15 months.
Police have refused to release any details about how Ms Glennon was murdered, pending a post mortem examination today.
The body of 23-year-old Jane Rimmer was found in bush south of Perth, last August, two months after she vanished from Claremont.
The first woman to vanish, in January 1996, was 18-year-old Sarah Spiers, who's still missing.
CONSUMER'S ASSOCIATION SAYS BANK MERGER WILL COST CUSTOMERS
The Australia Consumers Association says the US experience shows the supposed saving from banks merging and closing branches do not get passed on to customers.
The association's Mara Bun says the planned takeover of the Bank of Melbourne by Westpac will actually cost the bank's customers money.
Ms Bun says a survey last month showed Westpac charges are between $25 and $85 a year more than the Bank of Melbourne's.
Yesterday's announcement of the Westpac bid, which still needs Federal Government approval, saw Bank of Melbourne shares rise 70 cents.
Westpac is offering 1.4 billion dollars for the company and denies competition will be reduced and that customers will be worse off.
FOOD COUNCIL SAYS PREVENTION IS THE KEY TO FOOD SAFETY
The Australian Food Council says more restrictive regulation of the food industry and extra inspectors is not the solution to food safety problems.
Council executive director Mitchell Hooke says the development and implementation of standards - for the production, preparation and sale of food - must be accelerated.
Mr Hooke says the recent incidents of food contamination underscore the need for an innovative system of food hygiene regulation that keeps pace with technological and structural changes.
He says many food manufactureres have developed their own preventative systems.
SMALL EARTHQUAKE ROCKS MELBOURNE
A minor earth tremor shook parts of Melbourne's outer south-eastern suburbs overnight but sound sleepers would have missed the event.
RMIT Seismologist, Gary Gibson, says the quake, measuring just over two on the Richter scale, occured in areas including Pakenham and Cranbourne, around half past two.
Mr Gibson says a two is a small earthquake that is over in less than a second and is heard rather than felt.
He says the quake would have sounded like a distant explosion.
NSW POLICE HOLD MEETING ON REFORMS
The New South Wales Police Commissioner will hold a state-wide phone link-up with police this morning, to discuss reforms to the service.
Commissioner Peter Ryan will field questions from 13,000 officers, who'll attend the meeting at 200 locations around the state.
The Commissioner's office says the aim of the tele-conference is to update police on the progress of reforms begun in line with the Police Royal Commission recommendations.
FIERCE COMPETITION EXPECTED AS PATROL BOATS GATHER
Competition between Australian Navy patrol boat crews is expected to be fierce during an exercise off the coast of Darwin, which will see the largest gathering of patrol boats in several years.
Eleven patrol boats, a guided missile frigate and a naval tanker will sail into Darwin Harbour from today in the lead-up to the five-day exercise which starts on Monday.
The exercise is aimed at practicing and refining patrol boat operations including live firings, and test boarding and search procedures.
Over the past year the Navy 'watchdogs' have caught more than 100 foreign boats fishing illegally within Australian waters.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
